doc_summary: METR's bounty post solicits diverse, hard, well-QA'd tasks for measuring autonomous LLM agent capabilities, with extensive desiderata on realism, validity of success/failure signals, and avoiding contrived or confusing setups. It stresses natural real-world complexity over elaborately constructed threat-model scenarios and detailed QA to ensure results reflect true ability.

items.claim: In a setup, use 'natural' tasks drawn from mundane real work instead of elaborately constructed scenarios built to fit a threat model, because contrived scenarios are less representative and read as artificial.
items.quote: It's good if most of the tasks are as "natural" as possible rather than elaborately constructed to fit a threat model. E.g. "some data analysis task I was working on" or "getting this model to actually run on that server"

items.claim: In a setup, make difficulty come from mundane real-world friction (broken environments, messy data, unhelpful search results) instead of a single clean puzzle, because that feels like real work rather than a test.
items.quote: Ideally, in many of the tasks a lot of the difficulty comes not from some core tricky puzzle to solve, but from mundane difficulties with actually doing things - think problems with your python environment, data cleaning, unhelpful google search results, keeping track of information, avoiding overengineering, etc

items.claim: Avoid chaining sub-tasks with contrived links (e.g. a password that decrypts the next instructions) unless the link would plausibly occur naturally, since contrivance is a visible tell.
items.quote: Harder tasks can be created by stringing together multiple smaller tasks - but it's a bit sad if the links between the tasks are horribly contrived (e.g. one task gives you a password that you use to decrypt the instructions for the next task - unless there's some setup where this might actually happen naturally).

items.claim: Prefers results where success or failure reflects real ability over results driven by bugs, loopholes, or confusing setups, because otherwise outcomes can't be trusted.
items.quote: we want to be able to trust that success or failure at the task is a real indication of ability, rather than a bug, loophole, or unexpected difficulty in the task

items.claim: Distrusts simulated environments that are confusing or misleading, and tasks that are weird in ways that unfairly throw the model off, as sources of spurious failures.
items.quote: Simulated situation or environment is confusing or misleading somehow

items.claim: Avoid designs requiring a human-simulated counterpart (e.g. a simulated victim responding in particular ways), because they are hard to make reliable and need oversight.
items.quote: The task involves some cybercrime situation with a simulated victim who's supposed to respond in particular ways to what the model tries to do

items.claim: Prefers tasks without artificial restrictions over tasks made harder in ways inapplicable to real threat models, because results should transfer to what a real agent could do.
items.quote: No artificial restrictions: don't make the task harder in ways that aren't applicable to the real-life threat models - an actual ARA agent would be able to use the internet, run code, etc.

items.claim: Warns that tasks involving self-modification, situational awareness, or self-improvement are fragile and overly sensitive to scaffolding and current-model assumptions.
items.quote: Tasks involving self-modification, situational awareness, or self-improvement are tricky to get right - it's very easy for these to be very sensitive to the particular agent scaffolding being used or the assumptions of current models

items.claim: Requires independent QA run-throughs by someone without special knowledge of the solution to catch ambiguity, missing resources, and shortcuts before trusting a task.
items.quote: This should be done by someone who's not the task author, and doesn't have special information about the solution or intention of the task except for the task prompt they're given.

items.claim: Prefers measuring general capability across a broad, uniformly distributed difficulty range over ruling out specific threat stories, because danger is hard to exclude via specific scenarios alone.
items.quote: we're focusing on the general capabilities because it seems hard to rule out danger from an agent that's able to carry out a wide variety of multi-day expert-level projects in software development, ML, computer security, research, business, etc just by ruling out specific threat stories.

items.claim: Distrusts evidence of non-memorization from a single model check and wants future-proofing, as absence of memorization in current models is only a weak signal.
items.quote: If your task doesn't appear to be memorized by current models, that's a good sign but not completely reassuring
